newsitem.title: USA: New, real-time animation muscles way into Toonland.
newsitem.headline: New, real-time animation muscles way into Toonland.

text.p: "Hercules" animators move over. A new breed of film and television artists is moving into Toonland.

Walt Disney Co.'s "Hercules" may be the hottest animated movie in the country this week, but drawing and painting animated cels, then putting them on film -- even if the process is now speeded with the help of computers -- is increasingly more costly and time-consuming.
As a result, many producers are turning to an emerging wizardry called real-time animation.
Real-time characters are first modelled on a computer, then actors and sometimes puppeteers -- dressed in sensor-filled bodysuits and gloves -- supply movement to those characters.

As the actor raises an arm, the suit's sensors send a signal to the computer that tells the character to raise an arm. If the actor raises an eyebrow, so does the character. The same applies for hands, hips, feet and so on.
The result is an animated character with nearly human-like qualities.

"I love hand animation, and we're not trying to compete with hand animation. But (real-time) characters represent a new art form," Chris Walker, president of Modern Cartoons Ltd., told Reuters in a recent interview.

Modern Cartoons and rival MediaLab U.S. are two of the most active companies in Los Angeles producing real-time animated characters. Both are proving the process, after about eight years of development and interest primarily only in Europe, can work now in Hollywood.

Both are in talks to produce network shows in the 1997-98 television season. And this fall, television network NBC will use a real-time animated character on network TV. That character, a peacock named "Johnny Chimes", was created by MediaLab, and will be used to introduce NBC's fall lineup of TV shows.

An NBC spokesman said the network's decision to use real-time animation, among other reasons, primarily factored down to turnaround time for new commercials. Changes to on-air skits can be made in a matter of hours. In traditional cel animation and relatively new computer animation -- called keyframe animation -- changes often take weeks to complete.

MediaLab, which opened its Los Angeles office in January, can produce 20 minutes of animation in one day vs. two to five seconds a day for keyframe animation. Moreover the cost, which is as high as $1,000 per minute for MediaLab, can run up to $1,500 per second for keyframe.
Computers were used to produce Disney's popular movie, "Toy Story," and were also used in portions of "Hercules".
Those movies, however, took the collaboration of hundreds of individuals and years of work on the computer and in production studios.

Modern Cartoons can render characters with two people -- one on the computer and one in the suit. A 30-minute TV show it is developing will take a total of about 30 people from planning through finished product, Walker said.

MediaLab uses an actor in the suit, two puppeteers to control facial movements and a person at the computer controls. But the result on screen is essentially the same -- compelling characters that are entertaining but also cheap and fast to produce.
"(We) give the studios animation on their own terms," said MediaLab Executive Producer Mackenzie Waggaman. "We seem to have tapped into a situation with tremendous upside."
